output.title: Why bananas brown faster next to other fruit
output.summary: Ripe fruit releases ethylene gas. Nearby bananas detect it and ripen faster, which leads to faster browning.
learningObjectives: Explain that ripening fruit releases ethylene gas
Explain that ethylene tells nearby bananas to ripen and brown faster
misconceptionNotes: Brown spots do not always mean the banana is rotten or unsafe; very ripe browning is normal ripening, though moldy or fermented smells mean it should be thrown out.

steps.title: Yellow alone, brown in a crowd
steps.text: A banana alone on the counter stays yellow for days. Put it in a bowl touching apples or avocados, and in a day or two it gets spots, then turns soft and brown. The puzzle is: the other fruit never touches the inside of the banana, so how does it change it?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Other ripe fruit releases an invisible gas called ethylene. Your banana breathes it in, and that gas tells the banana to ripen and brown faster.

steps.title: Action at a distance needs a messenger
steps.text: First truth: to change something without touching it, something must travel between them. In a fruit bowl there is only air, heat, and light. Heat and light from an apple are tiny. So we look for something that moves through air: a gas.

guess.question: If fruit in a bowl can affect fruit it is not touching, how must the message travel?
options: By sending a message through the table
By moving through the air as a gas
guess.why: It must travel through the air as a gas, because there is no other connection between the fruits.

steps.title: Living things talk with chemistry
steps.text: Second truth: living things use chemical messages. A plant hormone is one of those messages. Jargon check: hormone just means a chemical that tells cells to start or stop a job, like soften, sweeten, or change color.

guess.question: A plant hormone is best thought of as what?
options: A chemical message that switches jobs on and off
A tiny heater that cooks the fruit
guess.why: A hormone is a chemical message that switches jobs on and off, like telling fruit to start ripening.

steps.title: Neighbors leak gas
steps.text: Ripe apples, pears, avocados, and bananas themselves all leak ethylene from their skin. It is normal, not rot. So in a crowded bowl, the air holds extra ethylene from neighbors plus the banana's own gas.

guess.question: You have a ripe apple and a yellow banana. Which makes ethylene?
options: The apple and the banana both release ethylene
Only rotten fruit releases a gas, fresh fruit does not
guess.why: Both ripening fruits make ethylene, so the apple adds extra gas around the banana.

steps.title: The banana hears the signal
steps.text: The banana skin lets air in. When ethylene arrives, banana cells hear the signal and start ripening work: hard starch becomes sweet sugar, firm walls soften, and yellow skin thins.

guess.question: When ethylene reaches a banana, what jobs does it switch on?
options: Turn starch to sugar, soften, and change color
guess.why: Ethylene switches on ripening jobs: starch to sugar, softening, and color change.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: more fruit means more ethylene in the air. More ethylene means the banana ripens faster. Very ripe cells leak and let browning enzymes work, so spots spread faster. That is why the banana next to other fruit goes brown first.

guess.question: Why does faster ripening mean more brown?
options: Faster ripening leads to faster browning
Browning happens only if fruit are touching
guess.why: Faster ripening leads to faster browning because softening and enzyme action that make brown spots happen as the last stage of ripening.

steps.title: Bag test
steps.text: Safe test: take two same-yellow bananas. Leave one alone on the counter. Put the other in a loose paper bag with a ripe apple, folded shut. Check after 1 and 2 days. The bag traps gas, so the bagged banana should spot first. Do not use a sealed plastic bag for long, and throw out moldy fruit.

steps.title: Keep one banana fresh
steps.text: Think: grocers keep bananas cool and airy to ship them green. At home, where should you keep a banana you want to save? Use the same rule in reverse.

guess.question: If trapping ethylene speeds ripening, what should cold and fresh air do?
options: Ripen at the same speed as before
guess.why: Cold and fresh air should slow ripening, so the banana stays yellow longer because there is less signal and slower cell work.

steps.title: How the gas was found
steps.text: In the early 1900s, scientists noticed fruit near gas heaters ripened strangely and leaves fell off trees near leaking gas pipes. They traced it to ethylene in the gases. Later they found ripening fruit makes its own ethylene. That is why we now store, ship, and ripen bananas by controlling this gas.

steps.title: Use it in your kitchen
steps.text: Next time you shop, notice: some fruits like apples and avocados are heavy ethylene makers. Citrus and berries make much less. To slow browning, keep bananas away from heavy makers and out of warm closed bowls. To ripen a hard avocado, do the opposite and bag it with a banana.

claims.text: Many fruits, including bananas, apples, avocados, and pears, release ethylene gas as they ripen.
Ethylene is a plant hormone gas that signals fruit tissue to ripen faster.
Bananas are climacteric fruits, meaning they continue to ripen after picking and make extra ethylene during ripening.
Ripening in bananas involves starch turning to sugar, flesh softening, skin color change from green to yellow to brown, and flavor change.
Brown spots on bananas come from cell walls breaking down and natural enzymes causing browning reactions as the fruit gets very ripe.
Trapped ethylene around fruit in a bowl or bag raises ripening speed, while fresh air flow or cold slows it.
claims.uncertainty: Exact speed depends on amount of fruit, variety, temperature, and airflow; general effect is well supported.

claims.text: Ethylene was identified in the early 1900s as the gas from ripening fruit and burning gas that caused plants to drop leaves and fruit to ripen.

output.title: How a cactus saves water
output.summary: A cactus catches fast rain with wide roots, stores it in its fat stem, and saves it with waxy skin, spines, and resting in daytime heat.
learningObjectives: Living things need water and lose water to hot dry air.
A cactus stem stores water for dry times.
Spines, waxy skin, and wide roots help a cactus catch and keep water.
misconceptionNotes: A cactus still needs some water to live; it is very good at saving water, not living with zero water.

steps.title: A fat plant in a dry place
steps.text: Look at a cactus. It is fat, green, and prickly. It sits in hot, dry sand where other plants would droop. Puzzle: if there is almost no rain, how does it stay alive and juicy?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: A cactus saves rain water inside its fat stem, and it is very slow to let that water out. Kind correction: it does still need a little water — it is just a champion saver.

steps.title: Water runs away
steps.text: First truth: all living things need water. Second truth: water moves away into hot, dry air. Jargon check: lose means water leaves into the air. So desert life must catch water and stop it from leaving.

guess.question: What happens to a wet sponge left in hot sun?
guess.why: It dries out because water moves into dry air. The same drying happens to living things.

steps.title: Food needs air, air loses water
steps.text: Plants make food from sunshine, air, and water. To breathe in air, leaves have tiny mouths. Water can slip out of those mouths. Big soft leaves are great for catching sun, but bad in a desert because they lose lots of water.

guess.question: What do green plants do to make food?
options: Use sun + air + water to make food
guess.why: Use sun + air + water to make food is right. To take in air they open tiny mouths, and water can escape there.

steps.title: A bottle for a body
steps.text: The stem does the big job. It is thick and squishy inside. After rain, it fills up like a water bottle. Then the plant drinks from its own bottle when there is no rain.

guess.question: Which can hold more water?
guess.why: The fat cactus stem can hold more water because it is thick and spongy inside.

steps.title: Spines and skin keep water in
steps.text: Next, the coat keeps water in. Spines are tiny changed leaves. They do not lose much water, they shade the plant, and they keep thirsty animals away. Waxy skin works like a raincoat turned inside out — it keeps water from slipping out. Many cacti also rest in hot daytime and breathe more at cool night.

guess.question: Which loses less water in hot wind?
options: Sharp spines and thick waxy skin
guess.why: Sharp spines and thick waxy skin loses less water because small shape and wax keep water in.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: wide roots drink fast when rain comes, the fat stem stores it, and spines plus waxy skin save it. Catch fast, store lots, spend slow. That is how a cactus lives without much water.

guess.question: Rain falls fast and light in the desert. Which roots catch more?
options: Wide roots near the top of the soil
One tiny root in a cup
guess.why: Wide roots near the top of the soil catch more because they reach more rain over a big area.

steps.title: Grape versus slice
steps.text: Try with a grown-up: put a cut apple slice and a whole grape in the fridge uncovered for a day. Which dries out more? The slice is like a big leaf. The grape skin is like waxy cactus skin. See how skin protects water.

steps.title: Long dry time
steps.text: Think: no rain for a long time. What happens to the fat stem? Use what you learned about storing and saving.

guess.question: If it does not rain for many weeks, what will the cactus do?
options: It will use stored water and shrink a little
It will grow big new soft leaves right away
guess.why: It will use stored water and shrink a little because the stem can slowly give up saved water.

steps.title: How people figured it out
steps.text: Cacti grow wild mostly in dry parts of the Americas. People who lived there long ago watched them stay green after rain stopped. Later plant scientists cut them open, saw the wet spongy inside, and figured out: the stem is a water tank.

steps.title: Spot the folds
steps.text: Look next time: can you find folds on a cactus? When full of water they stretch out. When dry they pull in. What other desert savers can you find — thick leaves on other plants?

claims.text: Cacti grow in dry places like deserts where rain is rare and air is hot.
Plants need water to live, and they lose water to the air through tiny mouths used to take in air for making food.
A cactus stem is thick and fleshy and can hold extra water inside like a water bottle.
Cactus spines are changed leaves, and cactus skin has a waxy coat that slows water loss.
Many cacti have wide, shallow roots near the surface that quickly soak up rain when it falls.
Many cacti save water by keeping their tiny skin mouths closed in the hot day and opening them more at cool night.
claims.uncertainty: Exact timing varies by species; simplified for child level.

claims.text: Cacti grow wild mostly in dry parts of the Americas, and people learned about them by watching how they live there.

output.title: Why wrist veins look blue
output.summary: Blood is always red. Veins look blue because skin scatters blue light back while dark-red vein blood absorbs red light.
learningObjectives: Explain that vein blood is dark red, not blue
Use light absorption and scattering to explain why veins look blue through skin
Predict color changes when light or depth changes
misconceptionNotes: It is kind to think vein blood itself is blue because diagrams often color veins blue, but that blue is just a drawing code - real blood taken from a vein is dark red.

steps.title: Blue lines, red blood
steps.text: Look at the inside of your wrist. You see thin blue-green lines. But when you get a cut, even right over a vein, the blood that comes out is red. So why do the lines look blue if the blood inside is red?

steps.title: The quick answer
steps.text: Your blood is never blue. It is always red. Veins only look blue because you are seeing them through skin, which changes the light coming back to your eyes.

steps.title: Color is bounced light
steps.text: First truth: color is about light. White daylight holds all colors mixed together. When it hits something, that thing soaks up some colors and bounces the rest to your eyes. Jargon check: absorb means soak up, reflect means bounce back.

guess.question: When white light hits an apple, what decides that you see red?
options: It picks which colors bounce back to your eyes
guess.why: You see red because the apple absorbs most colors and reflects red to your eyes.

steps.title: Blood is built to be red
steps.text: Second truth: blood gets its color from hemoglobin. That is a protein with iron in your red blood cells that grabs oxygen. Hemoglobin soaks up blue-green light and bounces back red. With lots of oxygen it is bright cherry red. With less oxygen, like in most veins, it is dark brick red. Never blue.

guess.question: Blood full of oxygen vs blood with less oxygen: what colors are they really?
guess.why: Both are red: bright red with lots of oxygen, dark red with less oxygen, because hemoglobin with iron reflects red.

steps.title: Veins are buried pipes
steps.text: Your wrist veins are tiny return pipes sitting a little under the skin. Arteries bring bright-red blood out from the heart. Veins take darker-red blood back. You are not looking at bare blood; you are looking through skin, fat, and a vein wall.

guess.question: Which way does blood in your wrist veins flow?
guess.why: Veins carry blood back toward the heart, so wrist-vein blood is dark-red blood on its return trip.

steps.title: Skin filters the light
steps.text: Light has to travel down through skin and back up to be seen. Red light is long-wave: it dives deep and gets soaked up by the dark-red blood. Blue light is short-wave: it scatters more in skin and bounces back to your eyes without reaching as deep.

guess.question: Sunlight hits your wrist: which color is more likely to scatter back out of the skin to your eyes?
guess.why: Blue light scatters and bounces back out more easily, while red light dives deeper in.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the vein holds dark-red blood that soaks up lots of red light. The skin above scatters blue light back to you. Your eyes get more blue than red from that spot, so your brain reads the vein as blue or green. Take away the skin and the trick ends — the blood is red.

steps.title: Press and watch
steps.text: Try this safely: in bright daylight, look at veins on the back of your hand, then press fingertips lightly beside them to push a little blood away for a second. The blue look fades where blood is pushed out and returns when blood flows back. That shows you were seeing blood through skin, not blue paint in the tube.

steps.title: Why is a bruise blue?
steps.text: Check your thinking: a bruise is leaked red blood trapped under skin. Use the same rules. What should happen to the light?

guess.question: A fresh bruise looks blue-purple but turns brown-yellow as it heals. Why does it start blue-purple?
options: Because the bruise blood turned blue
Because blood trapped under skin filters light like a vein does
guess.why: Trapped red blood under skin absorbs red light while skin scatters blue back, same filter trick as veins.

steps.title: Who figured out it is a trick of light?
steps.text: In 1628 William Harvey proved blood goes around in a circle, pumped by the heart, so vein blood must be the same red blood coming back. Later scientists shined lights on skin and measured what bounced back, and showed the blue look comes from how skin and blood handle light — not from blue blood. School diagrams still color veins blue, which keeps the myth alive.

steps.title: From wrist to hospital sensor
steps.text: Want to go further? Hospitals use this light trick on purpose. A clip on your finger shines red and infrared light through skin to guess how much oxygen is in your bright-red vs dark-red blood. Next time you see a map with red arteries and blue veins, remember: those are labels, not photos.

claims.text: Human blood is always red because hemoglobin containing iron absorbs other colors and reflects red.
Blood with lots of oxygen is bright red and blood with less oxygen is dark red, but neither is blue.
Veins are blood vessels that carry blood back toward the heart and often lie a little below the skin surface.
White light is made of many colors, and the color we see is the light that bounces back to our eyes.
Skin and tissue scatter short blue wavelengths back out more easily, while longer red wavelengths go deeper in and get absorbed by blood.
claims.uncertainty: Exact shade depends on skin tone, fat, depth of vein, and lighting, so scientists describe this as a general optical effect rather than a fixed rule.

claims.text: William Harvey showed blood circulates in one loop pumped by the heart, which means vein blood must still be red blood on its way back.

output.title: Why does iron go orange and flaky?
output.summary: Iron turns orange and flaky because it joins with oxygen and water to make soft orange rust that cracks and falls off.
learningObjectives: Say that rust needs both air and water to form on iron.
Say that rust is a new orange stuff, not just dirty iron.
misconceptionNotes: Rust is not dirt sitting on the nail. It is the iron itself changing into new stuff.

steps.title: A shiny nail turns crumbly
steps.text: You see an old nail. It was gray and shiny and hard. Now it has orange spots. The spots feel rough and pieces fall off like crumbs. Why does strong iron turn into soft orange flakes?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: The iron joins with air and water to make new stuff called rust. Rust is orange and soft and breaks apart.

steps.title: Tiny pieces hold tight
steps.text: All things are made of super tiny pieces called atoms. You cannot see them. In iron, the iron atoms hold each other very tight, like building blocks. That is why iron is strong.

guess.question: Are the tiny pieces in strong iron stuck tight or loose?
guess.why: Stuck tight like building blocks is right, because that tight hold makes iron strong.

steps.title: Air and water touch everything
steps.text: Air is all around, even if you cannot see it. One part of air is called oxygen. Water from rain or damp air is often on the nail too.

guess.question: What is all around the nail outside?
guess.why: Air and water is right, because air is all around us and rain and damp add water.

steps.title: Iron changes into new stuff
steps.text: When iron sits wet for days, the iron pieces let go of each other and join with oxygen and water pieces. This joining makes new stuff. We call it rust. It is not dirt on top. The iron itself changes.

guess.question: When iron, air, and water meet for a long time, what happens?
guess.why: Makes new stuff is right, because the tiny pieces join and change into rust.

steps.title: Why orange and soft
steps.text: The new rust pieces look orange-brown. They do not hold each other tight. They swell up bigger than before, crack, and let air and water go deeper inside.

guess.question: What does the new stuff look and feel like?
guess.why: Orange and soft is right, because the new rust pieces hold light and hold each other in a new way.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: wet iron slowly changes to rust. Rust is orange, puffy, and weak, so it flakes off. Then new iron shows, and it rusts too. That is why the nail goes orange and flaky.

guess.question: If you leave the wet nail for a long, long time, what will happen?
options: it turns to orange crumbs and falls
guess.why: It turns to orange crumbs and falls is right, because more and more iron keeps changing to soft rust and flaking off.

steps.title: Two nails test
steps.text: Ask a grown-up to help. Take two clean iron nails. Put one in a dry closed jar. Put one in a cup with a little water, open to the air. Look each day for a week. Which one gets orange spots?

steps.title: Bikes in rain
steps.text: Think of two bikes. Same metal. One is kept dry inside. One is left in rain outside. Use what you learned. Which one rusts?

guess.question: One bike sleeps in a dry garage. One sleeps out in rain. Which gets more rust?
options: the dry bike stays shiny, the wet bike gets rusty
the dry bike gets rusty, the wet bike stays shiny
guess.why: The dry bike stays shiny, the wet bike gets rusty is right, because rust needs both air and water together.

steps.title: Who found the air part?
steps.text: Long ago people did not know why metal changed. About 250 years ago, a scientist named Antoine Lavoisier showed air has oxygen. He showed metals change when they join with that oxygen. That helped us explain rust.

steps.title: Stop the rust
steps.text: People keep iron dry with paint or oil to block air and water. Stainless steel mixes iron with other metals to slow rust. What in your home is painted to stop rust?

claims.text: Iron is a metal made of tiny pieces called atoms stuck together strong and shiny.
Air has oxygen in it, and wet air or rain adds water.
Rust forms when iron mixes with both oxygen and water to make a new stuff called iron oxide.
Iron oxide, or rust, is orange-brown in color.
Rust does not stick tight like iron does, so it gets soft, grows bigger, cracks, and flakes off.
Antoine Lavoisier helped show that air has oxygen and that metals change by joining with oxygen.

output.title: What actually burns in a candle?
output.summary: The wick is only a delivery straw. Heat melts the wax, capillary action pulls it up, it becomes vapor, and that vapor is what burns with oxygen.
learningObjectives: Tell fuel apart from wick: wax is the fuel, wick is the delivery tool.
Trace energy path: heat melts wax, wax becomes vapor, vapor burns.
Predict what stops a candle: no wax, no oxygen, or no heat.
misconceptionNotes: It looks like the wick burns because the flame sits on it, but the wick is mostly just a straw for melted wax; if only the wick burned, the candle would go out in minutes and the wax level would not drop.

steps.title: The string stays, the wax vanishes
steps.text: You light the little string on top, a yellow flame appears, and hour by hour the solid wax shrinks and disappears. The string stays about the same length, but the wax is gone. So what is actually disappearing into the flame — the string or the wax?

steps.title: Short answer: the wax
steps.text: The wax burns. The wick is just the holder — it brings melted wax up to the heat where the wax turns to gas and burns.

steps.title: Fire needs fuel plus air
steps.text: First truth: fire is not magic stuff. It is a chemical reaction called combustion — fuel joins with oxygen in the air and releases heat and light. No fuel + oxygen + heat = no flame.

guess.question: If you shut off both fuel and oxygen from a flame, what happens?
options: No, it would keep burning fine
No, it would go out for lack of fuel to react with oxygen
guess.why: It goes out for lack of fuel to react with oxygen — combustion is fuel reacting with oxygen to release heat and light, it cannot continue without both.

steps.title: Solid fuel must become gas to burn
steps.text: Second truth: solids do not burn well by themselves. To burn fast and bright, fuel must mix with air. That means solid wax must first melt to liquid, then heat up into an invisible gas called wax vapor. Jargon check: vapor just means fuel turned to gas.

guess.question: Wax is a solid full of carbon-hydrogen chains. What must happen before it can really burn in air?
options: Into a gas that can mix with air and burn
Into solid ash that cannot burn
guess.why: It must turn into a gas that can mix with air and burn — solids do not mix well with oxygen, but vapors do.

steps.title: The wick is a straw
steps.text: The wick is a straw, not the drink. Heat melts a little pool of wax. Tiny spaces between the wick fibers pull that liquid upward, just like water climbs a paper towel. Scientists call this capillary action.

guess.question: When wax melts into a little pool around the wick, where does the liquid go?
options: It runs down the outside of the candle
It climbs up the tiny gaps in the wick
guess.why: It climbs up the tiny gaps in the wick — the wick is like a tiny bundle of straws that pulls liquid up by capillary action.

steps.title: Melted wax becomes invisible gas
steps.text: At the top of the wick it is super hot. The liquid wax boils into invisible wax vapor. If you look closely, the blue part at the bottom of the flame is where this fresh vapor starts to mix with air.

guess.question: That liquid wax reaches the hot zone right under the flame. What happens to it next?
options: Turn straight to ash and smoke
guess.why: It turns to invisible wax vapor — the heat boils the liquid wax into a gas before it burns.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the yellow flame you see is burning wax vapor, not the string. That reaction makes the heat that melts more wax, which makes more vapor, which keeps burning. The wick chars a little at the tip, but it burns far too slowly to explain the big flame. Proof: when the wax runs out, the flame dies even though the wick is still there.

guess.question: If all the wax is gone but the wick is still there, what does the flame do?
options: The flame stays the same size
guess.why: The flame shrinks and dies — the vaporized wax is the main fuel, so without it there is almost nothing left to burn.

steps.title: Light the smoke, not the wick
steps.text: Try this with an adult: light a candle, let it burn 2 minutes, then blow it out. Right away, hold a lit match about 2 cm above the wick in the white smoke trail — do not touch the wick. The flame will jump down through the air and relight the candle. You just lit the trail of wax vapor, proving the fuel travels as a gas.

steps.title: A candle under a jar
steps.text: Use the same rules somewhere new. A candle under a sealed jar has plenty of wax and heat left, but only a little trapped air.

guess.question: You cover a burning candle with a clear glass jar sealed to the table. What happens after a few seconds?
options: It goes out because it runs out of oxygen
It burns brighter because glass traps heat
guess.why: It goes out because it runs out of oxygen — the wax vapor still there cannot burn without fresh oxygen, which shows combustion needs both fuel and air.

steps.title: Faraday and the candle lectures
steps.text: In 1860-1861 Michael Faraday gave six Christmas lectures for kids called The Chemical History of a Candle. He showed wax travels up the wick and burns as vapor, and that the flame makes carbon dioxide and water. It is still one of the most famous science demos ever.

steps.title: From candles to car engines
steps.text: Same idea runs engines and rockets: gasoline must spray into vapor, and a rocket must mix fuel with oxygen. Next time you see a sooty black tip on a candle jar, you know what it is — wax vapor that did not get enough oxygen to burn fully, leaving tiny carbon bits behind.

claims.text: A candle is a solid block of wax with a cotton-like wick running through the middle.
Burning (combustion) needs three things together: a fuel, oxygen from air, and enough heat to start and keep it going.
Heat from the flame melts nearby wax, and liquid wax is pulled up the wick by capillary action, like water climbing a paper towel.
The liquid wax gets so hot near the flame that it turns to invisible wax vapor (gas).
The bright flame is mostly burning wax vapor reacting with oxygen, which makes heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water vapor.
The wick chars at the tip but is not the main fuel; it acts as a holder that delivers melted wax to the flame.
Candle wax is made of hydrocarbon molecules, chains of carbon and hydrogen that store lots of chemical energy and burn easily as vapor.
Michael Faraday gave his famous lectures The Chemical History of a Candle in 1860-1861, showing that the wax is the fuel by careful experiments.

output.title: Why does ice float in my drink?
output.summary: Ice floats because frozen water spreads out and is less dense than liquid water.
learningObjectives: Say in own words that ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
Explain that ice is less dense because frozen water molecules spread out and take more room.
misconceptionNotes: Many children think all hard, solid things must sink. Kindly correct: hard does not mean dense. Ice is hard but spread-out inside, so it is less dense than liquid water and floats.

steps.title: Ice cubes that will not stay down
steps.text: You drop ice cubes in your drink. Clink! They do not fall to the bottom. They bob up to the top. Most hard things, like a rock or a spoon, sink. Why does this hard ice stay up?

steps.title: The quick answer
steps.text: Ice floats because ice is a little lighter than the same amount of water. It is less crowded inside.

steps.title: Everything is made of tiny pieces
steps.text: Everything is made of very tiny pieces. Scientists call them molecules. You cannot see them. They are like tiny building blocks.

guess.question: What is everything made of?
guess.why: Everything is made of tiny pieces called molecules packed together. That is why we can talk about how crowded they are.

steps.title: Crowded means dense
steps.text: Density means how crowded the tiny pieces are in one space. A crowded thing is dense. If it is more crowded than water, it sinks. If it is less crowded than water, it floats.

guess.question: You have two same-size boxes. One is crowded with toys. One has only a little. You put them in water. Which sinks?
guess.why: The crowded box sinks because more stuff packed in the same space means more dense, and more dense than water sinks.

steps.title: Water makes room when it freezes
steps.text: Water is special. In your drink, the water pieces slide and snuggle close. When water gets very cold and freezes, the pieces lock hands in an open shape. Like kids making a big circle with arms out.

guess.question: When water freezes into ice, what do the tiny water pieces do?
options: they hold arms out and make open space
guess.why: They hold arms out and make an open pattern with empty space, so ice takes up more room than the same water as a liquid.

steps.title: Same stuff, bigger box
steps.text: So the same water pieces take up MORE room as ice. Same pieces, bigger box. That means they are less crowded. Less crowded means less dense.

guess.question: Same water pieces. Which takes up more room, the ice cube or the melted water?
options: Ice, because the same pieces take up more room
Liquid water, because it is hot
guess.why: Ice takes up more room because its open shape spreads the same pieces wider, so ice is less dense.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: ice is less crowded than liquid water. Less dense things float. So ice floats in your drink. That is why the top sticks out and most hides just under the top.

steps.title: Watch it melt
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Fill a clear cup with water. Mark how high the water is. Gently put in one ice cube. Mark the new high spot. Wait until it melts. Does the water go way, way higher? No! It stays about the same, because the ice was already most of that melted water floating there.

steps.title: Big ice, little ice
steps.text: Big or small, hard does not mean sink. If it is ice and the drink is water, it floats. Can you guess what a tiny chip and a giant block both do?

guess.question: If you pour the same drink into a big bowl and put in a tiny ice chip and a huge ice block, what will they do?
options: It will sink to the bottom
It will still float on top
guess.why: Both will still float on top because both are made of ice, which is less dense than liquid water, no matter the size.

steps.title: The man in the bath
steps.text: Long, long ago, a thinker named Archimedes lived in Greece. He studied why things float in water. He found that water pushes up on things in it. That push lifts things that are less dense, like ice.

steps.title: Icebergs are giant ice cubes
steps.text: This matters far away too. In the cold ocean, huge ice mountains called icebergs float the same way. Fish can swim under them all winter because the ice stays on top like a blanket.

claims.text: Everything around you is made of very tiny pieces called molecules that are always moving.
Density means how much matter is packed into a space, and an object floats in a liquid if the object is less dense than the liquid.
When water freezes, its molecules make an open, spread-out pattern that takes up more space than the same molecules as liquid water.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, about 917 kg per cubic meter compared to about 1,000 for liquid water, so ice floats on liquid water.
Archimedes of Syracuse in the 3rd century BCE described buoyancy, the upward push of a fluid that makes less-dense things float.

output.title: What is in this glass?
output.summary: Your glass holds water, a clear liquid made of tiny moving H2O pieces.
learningObjectives: Say that the glass holds liquid water, not nothing.
Say water is made of tiny H2O pieces that move.
Explain why water looks clear and takes the shape of the glass.
misconceptionNotes: Clear does not mean empty: the glass looks see-through but it is full of water.

steps.title: A glass that looks empty
steps.text: You see a clear glass. You can see right through it. But it is not empty. It feels heavy and wet if you tip it. So what is the clear stuff inside?

steps.title: The short answer
steps.text: In the glass is water. Water is a liquid made of super-tiny pieces called H2O.

steps.title: Everything is made of tiny pieces
steps.text: Everything around you is made of matter. Matter is made of super-tiny building blocks. They are too small to see, even with a school microscope.

steps.title: Tiny groups called molecules
steps.text: A molecule is a tiny group of even tinier pieces joined together. A water molecule is called H2O. H means hydrogen. O means oxygen. Each one has 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen.

guess.question: If we could shrink down and look inside water, what would we see?
guess.why: We would see lots of tiny moving pieces, because water is made of molecules that move and slide past each other.

steps.title: Sliding pieces can flow
steps.text: In water, the H2O pieces hold on a little, but they can slide past each other. That is what makes water a liquid. It can flow and pour.

guess.question: What does water do when you pour it in a glass?
options: It flows and takes the shape of the glass
It keeps the shape of a block
guess.why: It flows and takes the shape of the glass, because liquid molecules stay close but can slide past each other.

steps.title: Why it looks clear
steps.text: Light from the room goes right through the water to your eyes. That is why it looks clear. Clear does not mean empty. The water is really there.

guess.question: Why can you see through the water?
guess.why: Light goes through it, because water lets most light pass, so it looks clear.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the glass holds back the sliding H2O pieces. They take the round shape of the glass. Light shines through, so you see a clear drink. That clear drink is water.

steps.title: Pour and watch
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Pour a little water from the glass into a bowl. Watch what happens. Does the water keep the tall glass shape, or make a new wide shape? Tap the glass gently. Does the water wiggle?

steps.title: Heavy and sloshy
steps.text: Think about air and water. Both are clear. But water is heavy and sloshes. Air is light and does not slosh. How could you tell which glass has water without tasting?

guess.question: Mia has two clear glasses. One has water. One has nothing, just air. She lifts them. One is heavy and sloshes. Which one is water?
guess.why: Water is the heavy one that sloshes, because water is matter with weight that flows like a liquid.

steps.title: Who found the tiny pieces?
steps.text: Long ago people did not know what water was made of. About 250 years ago, a man named Henry Cavendish made water by burning a gas called hydrogen. Soon Antoine Lavoisier showed water is hydrogen plus another gas called oxygen.

steps.title: The same water travels
steps.text: Next, ask: where did this water come from? All the water on Earth gets used again and again. The water in your glass was once rain, once a river, and maybe once drunk by a dinosaur. What will it become next?

claims.text: Water at room temperature is a liquid that flows and takes the shape of its glass.
All water is made of super-tiny pieces called molecules, and each water molecule is made of 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
Molecules in liquid water stay close together but keep moving and sliding past each other.
Pure water looks clear because visible light mostly passes through it, and tap water also holds tiny bits of dissolved air and minerals.
In the 1780s Henry Cavendish showed water forms when hydrogen burns, and Antoine Lavoisier showed water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.

problems.problem: Two options are not possible answers to which glass is water.

output.title: Why salt grains are little cubes
output.summary: Salt looks cubic because it is cubic inside: + Na and - Cl ions alternate in 3 directions, building a cubic lattice that grows into cube-shaped grains.
learningObjectives: Salt is Na+ and Cl- ions, not single NaCl molecules floating alone.
Opposite charges make ions stack in an alternating up-down, left-right, front-back pattern.
That cubic inside pattern grows into cubic outside grains.
misconceptionNotes: Salt cubes are not cut by machines or made cube-shaped on purpose; the cube shape grows by itself from how the ions fit together.

concepts.label: ion - an atom with electric charge
ionic bond - pull between + and - ions
crystal lattice - repeating 3-D stack of particles

steps.title: Tiny boxes
steps.text: Shake some table salt onto dark paper and look close. Many grains are tiny, see-through boxes with flat sides and square corners. Why boxes? Why not balls or random lumps? That is the puzzle.

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: Salt grains are little cubes because salt is made of Na+ and Cl- ions stacked like an alternating 3-D checkerboard. That inside stack is cubic, so the outside grain grows cubic too.

steps.title: Salt is crowds of ions
steps.text: First truth: matter is made of tiny particles. A salt grain is not one particle. It is trillions of even tinier particles called ions. An ion is an atom with an electric charge. Table salt has two kinds: positive sodium ions (Na+) and negative chloride ions (Cl-). Jargon check: Na+ means a sodium atom missing one electron, so it is +; Cl- means a chlorine atom with one extra electron, so it is -.

guess.question: If you could zoom into one salt grain, what would you find?
options: many Na+ and Cl- ions stacked together
guess.why: You would find many Na+ and Cl- ions stacked together, because a salt grain is a crystal made of huge numbers of ions.

steps.title: Opposites attract
steps.text: Second truth: opposite electric charges attract, like charges push away. So Na+ and Cl- pull toward each other. That pull is called an ionic bond. It is not fussy about direction — a + ion will hug any - neighbor it can reach.

guess.question: A + ion and a - ion are near each other. What do they do?
options: push far apart and fly away
guess.why: They stick close together, because opposite electric charges attract.

steps.title: Alternate to fit
steps.text: Now imagine building with + and - magnets. You would not put all the + together — they would repel. You would alternate them: + next to -, next to +, like a checkerboard. Salt does the same thing, but in 3-D: left-right, up-down, and front-back.

guess.question: To keep attractions high and repulsions low, how should + and - ions arrange?
options: all the + ions clump on one side and all the - on the other
guess.why: They should take turns + - + - in every direction, so every + is next to - ions and no + is forced against another +.

steps.title: Six hugs make a cube
steps.text: Because space has three directions, each ion can hold 6 opposite neighbors at once: one up, one down, one left, one right, one front, one back. Same-size + and - take turns at exactly equal spacing. That makes every corner a right angle. Scientists call this repeating stack a cubic lattice.

guess.question: In the middle of a salt crystal, how many closest opposite neighbors does one ion touch?
options: 6 opposite neighbors: up, down, left, right, front, back
only 1 opposite neighbor, like a pair
guess.why: 6 opposite neighbors, because space has 3 directions and each has two sides, and salt fills all of them with alternating ions.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: new ions landing from salty water join where attraction is strongest — in line with the rows already there. Straight rows grow into flat faces. Flat faces meeting at right angles grow into a cube. So the little cube you see is just the inside alternating pattern made big enough to see.

guess.question: If you keep adding alternating layers up-down, left-right, front-back, what outside shape do you grow?
options: a round ball with bumpy sides
a box with flat sides meeting at right angles
guess.why: A box with flat sides meeting at right angles, because new layers follow the same straight rows and flat planes as the lattice inside.

steps.title: Grow your own cubes
steps.text: Try this safe test: dissolve 3 spoonfuls of plain salt in a little hot water with an adult, pour into a shallow dish, and leave it still for 2-3 days. Do not stir. Check daily with a magnifier. You should see tiny square boxes starting on the bottom and sides. Stirred or fast-dried salt makes small broken lumps; still, slow water makes clearer cubes — proof shape comes from orderly stacking.

steps.title: Why salt snaps square
steps.text: Use the same idea somewhere new: breaking. If you crack rock salt, it does not smear. It pops into smaller rectangles. Why? The lattice has flat planes where a small shift would put + next to + and - next to -, which repel. So it splits cleanly along cube faces.

guess.question: You tap a large salt crystal with a hammer (with eye protection). What happens?
options: break along straight lines into smaller boxes
guess.why: It breaks along straight lines into smaller boxes, because the weak planes run between layers of same-charge ions that repel once shifted.

steps.title: Seeing with X-rays
steps.text: No one could see atoms 100 years ago, so how did we learn this? In 1913 William Bragg and his son Lawrence Bragg shone X-rays at salt and other crystals. The X-rays bounced off the rows of atoms and made spot patterns. From the spots they measured the spacing and proved salt is regular repeating layers, not a jumble. They won the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics.

steps.title: Beyond table salt
steps.text: Not every crystal is cubic. Sugar, snowflakes, and diamonds stack differently, so they grow different shapes. Next time you see kosher salt flakes or popcorn salt powder, ask: was it grown fast, broken up, or grown slow? Same stuff inside, different history outside.

claims.text: Table salt is sodium chloride, made of sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl-) in a 1 to 1 ratio.
Na+ is positively charged and Cl- is negatively charged, and opposite charges pull toward each other to form ionic bonds.
In solid salt, Na+ and Cl- stack in an alternating 3-D checkerboard where each ion is surrounded by 6 ions of the opposite charge: up-down, left-right, front-back.
This repeating pattern is a cubic lattice, so the building block and the way salt breaks are at right angles.
A crystal's outside shape reflects its inside atomic arrangement, and slow growth from water lets flat cube faces form.
In 1913-1915 William and Lawrence Bragg used X-ray diffraction to work out the atomic arrangement of crystals including sodium chloride, showing atoms sit in regular repeating rows.

output.title: Why a cut apple turns brown
output.summary: A cut apple turns brown because air touches the inside and an enzyme helper joins air with apple juices to make brown color.
learningObjectives: Tell that brown on cut apple is apple chemicals joined with air, not dirt.
Tell that cutting lets air in and an enzyme helper speeds the color change.
misconceptionNotes: The brown is not dirt and does not mean the apple just turned bad right away. It is the apple itself changed by air.

steps.title: A white apple turns brown
steps.text: You cut an apple. Inside it is white and juicy. After a few minutes it turns brown. Why did it change? It is not dirt. What touched it?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Cutting lets air touch the apple. Air joins with the apple and makes brown color.

steps.title: Air can change things
steps.text: Air is all around. Air has a gas called oxygen. Oxygen loves to join with other things. When it joins, colors can change. This joining is called oxidation.

guess.question: What is touching the cut apple?
guess.why: Air with oxygen touches it. Oxygen can join with things and change their color.

steps.title: The apple has special juices
steps.text: Inside an apple are tiny natural juices. They are safe. They are made to join with air. Bananas and pears have them too. Rocks and glass do not.

guess.question: Which things turn brown in air like this?
guess.why: Apples, bananas, and pears turn brown. They have the same kind of natural chemicals that join with air.

steps.title: Tiny fast helpers
steps.text: The apple also has tiny helpers called enzymes. An enzyme is like a fast worker. It helps the air and the juices join very fast.

guess.question: What does the apple helper, the enzyme, do to browning?
guess.why: It speeds it up. Without the helper, browning would be much, much slower.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Skin keeps air out. Cut breaks the skin. Air rushes in. The helpers get to work. The juices join with air and turn brown. Put it together: cut + air + helpers = brown apple.

steps.title: Test two pieces
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Cut an apple into 2 pieces. Put lemon juice on one. Leave one plain. Wait 15 minutes. Which stays white longer? The sour juice slows the helpers.

steps.title: No air, no brown?
steps.text: Think: what if no air can touch it? If we block air, can the brown still come fast?

guess.question: If you wrap a cut apple tight in plastic with no air, what happens?
guess.why: It stays white longer because less air can touch it to join with the apple.

steps.title: Finding the helpers
steps.text: Long ago, people saw cut fruit turn brown but did not know why. Later, scientists learned about enzymes, tiny helpers in living things that speed changes. Then they found an apple enzyme causes this browning.

steps.title: Cold and heat
steps.text: Next time, ask: does cold slow it too? Try one piece in the fridge and one warm. What do you see? Heat and cold change how fast helpers work.

claims.text: Air around us contains oxygen gas.
Oxygen can join with other chemicals in a change called oxidation, which can change colors.
Living things make helper parts called enzymes that make some chemical changes go much faster.
A cut apple lets air touch the inside. An apple enzyme helps oxygen join with natural apple chemicals to make brown colors.
Keeping air away or adding sour lemon juice slows the browning because it slows the enzyme and the joining with oxygen.
claims.uncertainty: Exact slowing depends on apple kind and amount; general idea is supported.

claims.text: In the 1800s and 1900s scientists learned that enzymes in plants and animals speed up changes like browning.
claims.uncertainty: Broad history of enzyme discovery; not one single day for apple browning.

problems.question: Which things turn brown in air like this?
problems.problem: One option is not a possible answer because rocks and glass cups do not brown like apples do.

output.title: Why do bubbles have rainbow colours?
output.summary: White light holds all rainbow colors. A bubble bounces light off its front and back, and the two waves add or cancel to keep different colors where the film is thicker or thinner.
learningObjectives: Light that looks white is made of many colors.
Bubbles color light by bouncing it off two close sides.
Thicker and thinner spots pick different colors.
misconceptionNotes: The rainbow is not paint or dye in the soap - clear soap and water can make the colors just with light.

steps.title: A clear ball makes colors
steps.text: You blow a bubble. It looks clear, but then — pink! Green! Blue! Swirls move like a rainbow. There is no paint in there. So where do the colors come from?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Sunlight looks white, but it is really all rainbow colors mixed. The bubble skin picks out different colors in different spots.

steps.title: Light is a mix of waves
steps.text: First truth: white light is a mix. Sunlight looks white, but inside are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. Second truth: light moves like tiny waves. Red waves are longer. Blue waves are shorter.

guess.question: What is white sunlight really made of?
guess.why: White sunlight is many colors mixed together, so a bubble can pick some out to show.

steps.title: A bubble is a thin film
steps.text: Third truth: a bubble wall is super thin. Word to know: film means a very thin skin. A bubble is water with a soapy coat on the front and back.

guess.question: How thick is the bubble wall?
options: Thin like a tiny skin of water
guess.why: The bubble wall is a very thin skin of water with soap on both sides, much thinner than hair.

steps.title: Two bounces
steps.text: Light hits the bubble. Some bounces off the front skin. Some goes in and bounces off the back skin. So your eye gets two bounced waves.

guess.question: How many bounces of light does a bubble make?
guess.why: Light bounces off both the front and the back of the film, so we get two sets of waves to compare.

steps.title: Waves add or cancel
steps.text: When the two waves meet, they mix. If top meets top, that color gets bright. If top meets bottom, that color goes away. We call this add or cancel.

guess.question: What happens when the two waves meet?
options: They can add up or cancel out
guess.why: They can add up or cancel out: if tops line up they get bright, if top meets bottom they cancel.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the film is not the same thickness everywhere. Water slides down, so the top gets thinner. Each thickness keeps a different color and cancels the rest. That is why you see moving rainbows.

guess.question: If a spot on the bubble gets thinner, what happens?
options: It stays the same color forever
guess.why: It picks a new color, because a different wave size now lines up to stay bright.

steps.title: Watch a bubble change
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: blow a bubble and do not touch it. Just watch. Do the colors slide and change? Look at the top and bottom. Which part changes first? That shows the film getting thinner.

steps.title: What about oily puddles?
steps.text: Oil on water has no dye either, but it shines rainbow too. Use your rule to guess why.

guess.question: A thin bit of oil floats on a puddle in the sun. What do you see?
guess.why: You see a rainbow puddle spot, because oil is also a thin film that picks colors the same way.

steps.title: Who figured it out?
steps.text: Long ago, Isaac Newton looked closely at thin films and rings of color. In his book Opticks in 1704, he wrote down how thickness makes colors. Later people showed it is waves adding and canceling.

steps.title: Find more rainbows
steps.text: Next time you see bubbles, CDs, or shiny feathers, look for rainbows. Ask: where is the thin film? What two bounces could be mixing?

claims.text: White light from the sun is a mix of many colors.
Light travels as tiny waves, and different colors have different wave sizes.
A soap bubble skin is a very thin film of water with soap on both sides.
Light bounces off both the front and the back of the thin soap film.
The two bounced light waves can add up to make a color bright or cancel to remove a color.
Where the film is a little thicker or thinner, different colors stay bright, so you see rainbow swirls.
Water slowly drains down, so the top of a bubble gets thinner and its colors change with time.
claims.uncertainty: Exact draining is complex, but top-thinning over time is well observed.

claims.text: Isaac Newton studied the colors of thin films and described them in his book Opticks in 1704.

problems.question: A thin bit of oil floats on a puddle in the sun. What do you see?
problems.problem: The marked answer is incorrect; a thin oil layer in sunlight makes a rainbow spot, not a plain white spot.

output.title: Why thinner strings sound higher
output.summary: Thinner guitar strings are lighter per length, so tension can shake them back and forth faster, and faster vibration sounds higher.
learningObjectives: Link pitch to how fast a string vibrates.
Explain that thinner means less mass to move, so faster vibration at similar tension.
Predict how thickness, tension, and length change pitch.
misconceptionNotes: Thinner strings are not higher just because they are tighter; on a guitar they are often at similar or even lower tension, the main difference is they are lighter and easier to speed up and slow down.

steps.title: Six strings, two voices
steps.text: Look at an acoustic guitar: six strings run from the top down the neck to the body. The low thick strings boom low, the thin high strings ring high. Same wood, same pluck — why should width alone change the note?

steps.title: The short answer
steps.text: Short answer: thinner strings make higher notes because they are lighter, so they wiggle back and forth faster. Faster wiggle means higher pitch.

steps.title: Pitch means speed of shaking
steps.text: First truth: sound is vibration. Pitch is how fast it repeats. We count repeats per second as frequency. 100 repeats per second sounds low; 400 per second sounds higher.

guess.question: If a string vibrates back and forth 400 times per second instead of 100 times per second, what happens to pitch?
options: It sounds louder but same pitch
guess.why: It sounds higher, because pitch follows vibration frequency: more vibrations per second means higher note.

steps.title: Light things turn faster
steps.text: Second truth: heavy things are lazy to move. A thick string packs more mass into each centimeter. A thin string packs less. With a similar pull from tension, the lighter thin string can speed up, stop, and turn around quicker.

guess.question: You pull aside a heavy rope and a light thread with the same force, then let go. Which one changes direction faster?
options: Harder to push and slower to turn
Easier to push and quicker to turn
guess.why: The light thread changes direction faster, because less mass means the same pull produces quicker back-and-forth motion.

steps.title: Stretch, snap back, repeat
steps.text: A guitar string is tied down at both ends. Pluck it sideways and tension pulls it back toward straight. It overshoots, gets pulled back again, and keeps shaking. That repeat is the vibration your ear hears.

guess.question: A guitar string is fixed at both ends and plucked to the side. What does tension do next?
options: The string just moves and stays bent
It is pulled back to center, overshoots, and repeats
guess.why: It is pulled back to center, overshoots, and repeats, because tension pulls it back while its motion carries it past center again and again.

steps.title: The race of thick vs thin
steps.text: Now race them. Same length, similar tightness. The thick heavy string lumbers back and forth slowly: low frequency, low note. The thin light string darts back and forth quickly: high frequency, high note. Thickness matters because it sets weight per length.

guess.question: Two strings have the same length and pull, but one is thick and heavy, one is thin and light. Which completes one back-and-forth shake first?
options: They finish at the same time
guess.why: The thin string finishes first, because less mass per length lets it accelerate and reverse faster, so its frequency is higher.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: thin means less mass per length. Less mass means faster back-and-forth under the same kind of pull. Faster back-and-forth means higher frequency. Higher frequency means higher note. That is why the thin high-E string sings high and the thick low-E string growls low.

steps.title: Rubber-band guitar
steps.text: Try it safely: stretch a wide rubber band and a thin rubber band over an open box. Pluck each gently the same way. Listen: the thin one sounds higher. Now stretch the thin one a little tighter — it goes even higher, showing tension matters too.

steps.title: Change pitch without changing strings
steps.text: Guitar players do not only use thickness. Pressing a fret shortens the shaking part, and turning the peg tightens it. Both raise pitch without changing thickness. That fits the same rule: less mass to move or stronger pull means faster shaking.

guess.question: You love a thick low string but want it to play a higher note without swapping it. Which works?
options: Press the string down to make it shorter
guess.why: Press the string down to make it shorter works, because a shorter vibrating length has less mass to move and completes shakes faster, raising pitch.

steps.title: An old musical rule
steps.text: Long ago, people noticed this on harps and lyres. Greek thinkers linked musical notes to string lengths and thicknesses: halve the moving length or use a lighter string and the note jumps up. Guitar makers still use that old rule when they pick string sets.

steps.title: How low can you go?
steps.text: Go further: why do bass guitars have super thick, long strings? Using our rule, big mass and long length mean very slow vibration — perfect for super low notes. What would happen if you made a guitar string thinner than hair?

claims.text: An acoustic guitar makes sound when plucked strings vibrate and the hollow body makes that vibration louder.
The pitch we hear is set by vibration frequency: faster back-and-forth vibration makes a higher note.
For a string fixed at both ends, the main vibration frequency goes up with more tension and down with more mass per length or more length.
A thinner guitar string of the same material has less mass for each centimeter of length than a thicker string.
If tension and length are similar, the lighter thinner string snaps back faster and vibrates at a higher frequency, so it sounds higher.
Early stringed instruments showed that thinner, shorter, and tighter strings make higher notes, an idea explored in ancient Greek study of music and strings.
claims.uncertainty: Exact original discoverer is debated in histories, so this is a general attribution not a single experiment.

output.title: Why stained glass glows
output.summary: Old stained glass is bright because metals melted into the glass filter daylight, letting only one strong colour through.
learningObjectives: Explain that stained-glass colour is light passing through glass, not surface paint.
Link bright colours to metals that absorb some light colours and transmit others.
misconceptionNotes: Colour is mostly inside the glass itself, not painted on top like house paint. Painted details exist, but the bright reds, blues, and greens come from metals melted into the glass.

steps.title: A glowing wall
steps.text: You stand in a dim church and the window glows like jewels: deep blue robes, ruby red borders, golden yellow stars. The light does not bounce off it like a painting. It shines through it. The puzzle: glass is made from pale sand, so where does that strong colour come from?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Old glassmakers melted a pinch of metal into the glass. The metal soaks up some colours of daylight and lets only the bright colour through.

steps.title: Colour is what is left over
steps.text: First truth: colour is light. Daylight looks white, but it is a mix of many colours. When we see a bright red window, what reaches our eyes is mostly red light. The other colours were soaked up, or absorbed, inside the glass.

guess.question: If white light shines on a filter that soaks up all colours except red, what do you see on the other side?
options: It looks red because only red light gets through
guess.why: It looks red because only red light gets through. The colour we see is the light left after absorption.

steps.title: Glass filters light
steps.text: Second truth: glass does not make light. Plain glass is clear because it lets almost all light through. To get colour, you must add something that blocks, or absorbs, part of the light. In glass, tiny bits of metal do that job. We call them metal ions: metal atoms locked in the glass.

guess.question: What is the difference between clear glass and coloured glass?
options: Clear glass lets most light through, tinted glass blocks some colours
Clear glass makes its own light
guess.why: Clear glass lets most light through, tinted glass blocks some colours. Glass does not make light; it filters daylight.

steps.title: Blue and green from cobalt, copper, and iron
steps.text: The main method is called pot-metal glass. While the glass is liquid and very hot, the maker stirs in powdered metal oxide, like sugar in tea. You need very little. Cobalt gives a strong deep blue. Copper gives light blue or green, and in a different mix it can give red. Iron gives greens and browns.

guess.question: A glassmaker wants deep blue for Mary's robe. What does she stir into the hot melted glass?
guess.why: A pinch of cobalt-rich mineral. Even less than 1% cobalt absorbs yellow and green light and lets deep blue through.

steps.title: Red from gold, yellow from silver
steps.text: Red and yellow were the clever tricks. A trace of gold, far too small to see as metal, makes glass ruby red. For yellow, makers brushed silver compounds on finished clear glass and heated it again. The silver sinks in a little and turns the spot yellow. That is called silver stain.

guess.question: How did old makers get a glowing ruby red?
options: Ruby red from a trace of gold
guess.why: Ruby red from a trace of gold. Tiny gold particles absorb green and blue light and let red through.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: pale sand becomes bright colour because each piece of glass holds a pinch of metal. The metal absorbs all but one colour. Sunlight shines through, so the colour glows. Dark lead strips hold the pieces together like outlines in a colouring book, which makes each bright patch pop.

steps.title: Layer test
steps.text: Try this safely: on a sunny window, hold up coloured sweet wrappers or craft cellophane, one layer then two or three layers. One layer glows bright. More layers get darker. Old glass is the same: the same metal looks brighter in thin glass and darker in thick glass. Makers learned to make sheets even and thin for bright colour.

steps.title: Predict a new colour
steps.text: Check your thinking: the colour is in the glass, not on it. Use the filter idea to predict.

guess.question: If you melted cobalt into a batch of clear glass, what colour would the cold sheet be when you hold it to the sky?
options: It would look black because no light gets through
It would look clear or cloudy
guess.why: It would look blue. Cobalt absorbs other colours and transmits blue, so daylight through the glass looks blue.

steps.title: Monks and recipes
steps.text: People coloured glass since Rome, but big picture windows grew in medieval Europe around the 1100s and 1200s. Around 1100 a monk called Theophilus wrote down recipes: melt sand with ash, add copper, cobalt, or gold for colour, cut sheets, join with lead. We still use his book to understand old windows.

steps.title: Look through, not at
steps.text: Next time you see a window, look closely. True old colour goes all the way through the glass - the edge of a broken piece is still coloured. Dark lines painted on the face are only details like eyes or folds in clothes. If you visit a museum, ask to see pot-metal glass and silver stain side by side.

claims.text: Stained glass gets most of its colour from tiny amounts of metals or metal oxides mixed into molten glass.
White daylight contains many colours of light, and the colour we see in stained glass is mainly the light that passes through it.
Plain glass lets almost all visible light through, so it looks clear or pale green.
Metal atoms in glass absorb some colours of light and let other colours through.
Cobalt makes deep blue, copper makes blue-green or red depending on glass chemistry, and iron makes green or brown.
A very small amount of gold makes ruby red, and silver compounds applied to the surface and heated make yellow to orange.
The colours look bright because sunlight shines through the glass, and dark lead strips between pieces help each colour stand out.
claims.uncertainty: Brightness also depends on thickness, daylight level, and church interior darkness; this is a simplification.

claims.text: Medieval makers in Europe from about the 12th century cut coloured glass into shapes and held them with lead strips; the monk Theophilus described adding metals for colour around 1100.
