output.title: Why paints make brown but lights make white
output.summary: Lights add colors to make white. Paints soak up colors to leave brown.
learningObjectives: Tell that light mixing adds light and paint mixing takes light away.
Explain in simple words why all lights make white and all paints make brown.
misconceptionNotes: It feels like paint and light should mix the same way, but they do opposite jobs: lights ADD light, paints TAKE AWAY light.

steps.title: Pretty colors turn yucky?
steps.text: Look at your palette. Red, blue, yellow, green — so pretty! You swirl them all together. Oh no! It turns yucky brown. But you heard all lights mixed make bright white. Why do they do opposite things?

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: Lights ADD light, so more colors means brighter, up to white. Paints TAKE AWAY light, so more colors means darker, down to brown.

steps.title: White light is full
steps.text: First truth: white light is not empty. White light, like sunshine, is full of all rainbow colors. Second truth: your eyes only see light that comes IN to them.

guess.question: What is white light made of?
guess.why: White light is made of all the rainbow colors together, which is why it can light up everything.

steps.title: Paint picks light
steps.text: Paint does not make light. Paint picks light. Red paint SOAKS UP blue and green and yellow. It only BOUNCES red back to your eyes. Soak up means drink in and keep. Bounce means throw back out.

guess.question: White light shines on red paint. What does the paint do?
options: Bounces back red and soaks up the rest
guess.why: The paint soaks up all the colors except red. The red bounces to your eyes, so you see red.

steps.title: Lights add
steps.text: Mixing lights is ADDING. A red light sends red. A green light sends green. Together they send MORE light to your eyes. Add red, green, and blue light and you get white!

guess.question: You shine a red flashlight and a green flashlight on the same white wall. What happens?
guess.why: The lights add together on the wall, so the spot gets brighter with more colors, closer to white.

steps.title: Paints take away
steps.text: Mixing paints is TAKING AWAY. Yellow paint soaks up blue. Blue paint soaks up yellow and red. Mix them and together they soak up almost everything. Less light can bounce back.

guess.question: You mix blue paint into yellow paint. What happens to the light?
guess.why: Each paint soaks up more colors, so less light is left to bounce back and the mix looks darker.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: all lights = all colors SENT to your eyes = white! All paints = almost all colors SOAKED UP = only a little dim light left = brown!

guess.question: You mix all your paints together. Which colors are left to bounce back?
guess.why: The paints soak up almost everything, so only a little dim light is left, which we see as brown.

steps.title: Watch it get dark
steps.text: Try it safe with a grown-up. Paint two dots far apart: yellow and blue. Then slowly mix where they touch. Watch it get darker and greener, then brown. You are watching light get taken away!

steps.title: Hot shirt test
steps.text: Think somewhere new: summer shirts. White shirts bounce lots of light away. Black shirts soak up lots of light. Which one gets hotter in the sun?

guess.question: On a sunny day, what color shirt will feel hottest?
options: White, because the shirt sends all light
Black, because the shirt soaks up all light
guess.why: A black shirt soaks up almost all the light and turns it to heat, while a white shirt bounces most light away.

steps.title: Newton and the rainbow
steps.text: Long ago, Isaac Newton let sunshine through a glass triangle called a prism. It split white light into a rainbow. Then he put the rainbow back together into white light. White was a mix all along!

steps.title: Screens and printers
steps.text: Screens ADD light with tiny red, green, and blue dots. Printers TAKE AWAY light with cyan, magenta, yellow, and black ink. Next time you watch TV or print a picture, you are using both kinds of mixing!

claims.text: White light, like sunlight, is made of many colors mixed together.
We see a thing's color from the light that bounces off it and goes into our eyes.
Mixing colored lights adds more light together, and red plus green plus blue light looks white.
Paint gets its color by soaking up some colors of light and bouncing back the rest.
Mixing many paints makes the mix soak up more and more colors, leaving only a little dim brown light to bounce back.
Isaac Newton showed with a glass prism that white light can split into rainbow colors and that colors can join back to white light.

output.title: Why big drums go boom
output.summary: A big drum sounds deeper because its big skin shakes more slowly, and slow shakes make low sounds.
learningObjectives: Sound is back-and-forth shaking called vibration.
Slow vibrations make low, deep sounds.
A bigger drum skin shakes more slowly, so it sounds deeper.
misconceptionNotes: Bigger does not just mean louder. A big drum can be soft and still sound deep. Deep means low pitch, not loud.

steps.title: Big boom, little ting
steps.text: You see a big drum and a little drum. Tap-tap! The little one goes ting-ting. The big one goes boom-boom. Why does the big one sound so deep?

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: A bigger drum sounds deeper because its big skin shakes more slowly. Slow shakes make low, deep sounds.

steps.title: All sounds are shakes
steps.text: Rule 1: Sound starts with a shake. We call that shake a vibration. No shake, no sound. The shaking pushes the air to your ear.

guess.question: When something makes a sound, what is it doing?
guess.why: It shakes back and forth. Sound starts as a vibration, a fast wobble.

steps.title: Fast is high, slow is low
steps.text: Rule 2: Speed of the shake sets the pitch. Pitch means how high or low a sound feels. Fast shakes = high sound. Slow shakes = low, deep sound.

guess.question: Which shakes make a deep, low sound like a bear voice?
guess.why: Slow shakes make deep sounds. Fast shakes make high sounds, like a bird.

steps.title: The skin does the shaking
steps.text: A drum is a pot with a tight skin pulled over the top. You hit the skin. It wobbles up and down really fast. That wobble pushes the air.

guess.question: When you hit a drum, what part shakes to start the sound?
guess.why: The stretchy skin on top shakes. You hit it, it wobbles up and down and pushes the air.

steps.title: Big skin shakes slowly
steps.text: A big drum has a big, heavy skin. A little drum has a small, light skin. Big heavy things cannot bounce back and forth as fast. So the big skin shakes more slowly.

guess.question: A big heavy drum skin is like a big elephant on a trampoline. How does it bounce?
options: Slowly, like a big elephant jumping
Quickly, like a little mouse jumping
guess.why: Slowly, like a big elephant jumping. Heavy, big things are slower to move back and forth.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: You hit the big drum. Its big skin shakes slowly. Slow shakes make deep sounds. So the big drum goes BOOM. The small drum shakes fast, so it goes TING.

steps.title: Pluck and hear
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: stretch a rubber band over a box. Pluck it. Now stretch a short, tight piece and pluck. Which sounds deeper? The long loose one shakes slower and sounds lower, just like the big drum.

steps.title: What about bells?
steps.text: Think of bells in a church. Small bells ring high. Big bells ring low. Same rule as drums!

guess.question: A tiny bell goes ding. Which bell will go dong, low and deep?
guess.why: The huge heavy bell will go dong. Bigger, heavier shakers vibrate slower and sound deeper.

steps.title: Drums are super old
steps.text: Long, long ago, people all over the world made drums from logs and animal skins. Drums are some of the oldest instruments ever. Drummers noticed: giant drums went boom, tiny drums went tap.

steps.title: Big and small everywhere
steps.text: Listen around you. A big dog goes woof-woof. A tiny dog goes yip-yip. Big guitar strings sound low. Tiny strings sound high. Can you find three more big-and-small sounds?

claims.text: Sound is vibration moving through air to our ears.
Pitch is how high or low a sound feels, and fast vibrations make high pitch while slow vibrations make low pitch.
Bigger and heavier things that vibrate tend to move back and forth more slowly, with lower frequency.
A drum makes sound when you hit its stretched skin and the skin wobbles back and forth and pushes the air.
A bigger drum has a bigger, heavier skin that wobbles more slowly, so it makes a deeper, lower sound.
Drums are among the oldest musical instruments and have been used by people for thousands of years.

output.title: Why clay hardens and changes colour in a kiln
output.summary: Kiln heat permanently removes water, breaks down clay minerals, and welds grains into hard ceramic, while burning organics and rusting iron changes the colour.
learningObjectives: Explain that wet clay is soft because water separates tiny mineral plates
Explain that kiln heat causes permanent chemical change and bonding, not just drying
Explain colour change as burning off organics and oxidation of iron
misconceptionNotes: A kiln does not just dry clay faster — drying is reversible, firing is a permanent chemical change; soaked fired pot will not turn back to soft clay.

steps.title: Soft grey pot in, hard red pot out
steps.text: A fresh clay pot is cool, damp, grey or brown, and you can dent it with a fingernail. After a kiln firing it is hard, rings when tapped, holds water, and is often red-orange or buff-white instead of dark grey. It never goes soft again, even in water. Why does heat alone make it both harder and a new colour?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Heat drives water out for good and welds the tiny clay grains together, so the pot becomes stone-like. At the same time, burnt plant bits disappear and iron rusts to red or stays dark, which changes the colour.

steps.title: Tiny plates plus water means bendy
steps.text: First truth: matter is made of tiny pieces. Clay is made of very tiny flat plates stacked like cards. Key word: plastic means you can push it into a new shape and it stays. Water coats the plates and lets them slide, so wet clay is plastic.

guess.question: If tiny plates can slide easily over each other, what can you do with the lump?
options: It can be shaped without cracking
guess.why: Sliding plates let the lump change shape without cracking, which is plasticity and why wet clay can be shaped.

steps.title: Some heat changes undo, some do not
steps.text: Second truth: some changes undo easily, some do not. Melting ice undoes when cold returns. Baking cake does not un-bake. Key word: chemical change makes new stuff with new bonds. Kiln heat is hot enough — hundreds of degrees — to cause chemical change in clay.

guess.question: If heating locks two bricks together with new chemical bonds, what happens when they cool?
options: You need hotter heat to pull it apart
You need colder air to pull it apart
guess.why: New chemical bonds stay when cool; you need hotter heat or force to break them, so the change is permanent.

steps.title: Water leaves twice
steps.text: In the kiln, heat works in stages. First, around 100 C, loose water steams off — like air-drying, but faster. Then around 400-600 C, the minerals themselves lose bound water from inside their crystals. That collapses the slippy layers. The pot can never be plastic again.

guess.question: You soak a dry-but-unfired pot and a fired pot overnight in water. What happens to the fired pot?
options: It turns back to soft clay
It stays hard and keeps its shape
guess.why: The dry pot softens because only loose water left, while the fired pot stays hard because its minerals changed and bonded.

steps.title: Grains weld together
steps.text: Hotter still, about 800-1100 C, the touching grains sinter: edges weld together and a little glass forms between them. Key word: sinter means join powder by heat without fully melting. Pores shrink. The soft plates become one stiff, stone-like network that rings when tapped and holds water.

guess.question: If edges touch and partly melt together as it gets hotter, what holds the pot together after cooling?
options: Grains weld and glassy bridges form
guess.why: Edges weld and glassy bridges freeze solid, gluing the grains into one hard network.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: wet clay is slippy plates + water, so it is soft and dark. Kiln heat removes the water for good, breaks down the plates, then welds what is left into hard ceramic. Burnt organics vanish, and iron locked in the clay rusts red in air or stays grey-black without air. Hardness is new bonding; colour is cleaner minerals plus rusted or unrusted iron.

steps.title: Compare drying and firing
steps.text: Safe test with air-dry clay or mud: make two small balls. Let both dry fully — they go pale and hard. Drop one in water for an hour; it softens and falls apart. Imagine the second went through a kiln: it would sit in water for days and stay hard. That gap is the difference between drying and firing.

steps.title: Predict the colour
steps.text: Use the iron idea: potters control colour with air. Plenty of oxygen makes iron form red hematite. Starved of oxygen with smoke and fuel, iron forms dark grey-black oxides. Same clay, different air, different pot.

guess.question: You fire an iron-rich pot half-buried in sand, half open to kiln air. What colours do you expect?
options: Red where air reaches, dark where buried
Dark where air reaches, red where buried
guess.why: Open side gets oxygen so iron oxidizes red like rust; buried side lacks oxygen so iron stays dark.

steps.title: From bonfire to kiln
steps.text: People first fired pots in open bonfires about 10,000 years ago — hot enough to harden, but smoky and uneven. Enclosed kilns by around 3000 BCE held heat in and let air in through vents, reaching sintering heat and making reds and buffs more even and repeatable.

steps.title: Bricks to porcelain
steps.text: Next time you see brick, tile, or porcelain, ask: how hot and how much glass? Bricks are low-fired and porous; stoneware and porcelain are fired hotter until almost glassy, so they are stronger and waterproof even without glaze. Same hardening story, pushed further.

claims.text: Pottery clay is made of tiny plate-like clay minerals mixed with water; the water lets the plates slide so wet clay is soft and plastic.
Air-drying removes pore water and stiffens clay, but adding water can soften it again until it is fired.
Kiln firing above about 600 degrees C drives off chemically bound water from clay minerals and joins particles by sintering and partial glass formation, which cannot be undone by soaking in water.
Firing shrinks pores and bonds grains together, making fired pottery hard, rigid, and able to hold water.
Many clays contain iron compounds, and oxygen in the kiln oxidizes iron to red hematite while lack of oxygen leaves dark magnetite or wustite, so firing atmosphere changes colour.
Early pottery was fired in open bonfires and pits, and closed updraft kilns were developed by about 3000 BCE to reach higher, more controlled temperatures.
claims.uncertainty: Exact date varies by region; 3000 BCE is a widely used approximate date for early kilns in the Near East and China.

output.title: What is an abstract painting a picture of?
output.summary: An abstract painting is not a picture of a named object. It is paint, color, and shape arranged to create feeling, movement, or an idea.
learningObjectives: Explain in plain words why an abstract painting is not a picture of a named thing
Describe what an abstract painting is made of and what it can show instead
misconceptionNotes: It is natural to expect every painting must be a picture of something real. In abstract art the artist often did not intend a hidden object to find.

steps.title: Colors with no name
steps.text: You see paint on a flat surface: patches of color, lines, drips, or blocks. There is no clear person, house, tree, or dog. So the puzzle is: if there is no thing to name, what is this a picture of?

steps.title: The short answer
steps.text: It is not a picture of a thing. It is an arrangement of color, shape, and line made to give a feeling, movement, or idea.

steps.title: First truth: paint first
steps.text: Start with what you can check: a painting is stuff — paint — placed on a flat top, like canvas or paper. Sometimes the artist arranges that stuff to look like something else. Sometimes they do not.

guess.question: At the simplest level, what is any painting?
guess.why: The correct answer is paint on a flat surface, because every painting starts as material put down by a person before it becomes a picture of anything.

steps.title: Second truth: how you spot a thing
steps.text: Second truth: you name a thing by clues. Your eyes and brain look for edges, faces, shadows, and sizes that match things you know. jargon check: 'representational' means it gives those clues. 'abstract' means it does not try to.

guess.question: Why is it harder to name a thing in an abstract painting than in a photo?
options: It gives fewer clues like eyes, edges, and shadows
It gives clearer clues than a normal photo
guess.why: It gives fewer clues like eyes, edges, and shadows, because our brain names things by matching those clues, and abstract art leaves them out.

steps.title: Color and mark make feeling
steps.text: Part 1 is color and mark. Red can feel fast or warm. Dark blue can feel calm or heavy. Thick, rough paint can feel loud. Thin, soft wash can feel quiet.

guess.question: A painting is only red zig-zags and black dots, with no sky or people. What can it still do?
options: It uses bright, clashing colors to feel loud and busy
guess.why: It uses bright, clashing colors to feel loud and busy, because color, size, and placement alone can change mood and energy without showing an object.

steps.title: Placement makes movement
steps.text: Part 2 is placement. Shapes close together can feel crowded. Shapes tilted can feel like falling. Shapes balanced in the middle can feel calm. Your body reads balance even when there is no thing shown.

guess.question: If the artist wants the painting to feel shaky, how would they likely place the shapes?
options: Tilted and crowded to feel shaky
Straight and centered to feel shaky
guess.why: Tilted and crowded to feel shaky is right, because tilt, crowding, and lack of balance change how stable the arrangement feels to your eyes and body.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: So put it together: this is not a failed picture of a dog or a landscape. It is a picture of an effect — like calm, clash, joy, grief, or speed — built directly from paint, color, and placement. That is the answer the parts point back to.

steps.title: Test the feeling
steps.text: Try this safe test. Cover the title label. Look for 30 seconds and say only feeling words: calm, angry, playful, sad. Turn the image upside down and see if the feeling stays. If it stays, the feeling comes from colors and shapes, not from a hidden object.

steps.title: Squares, not houses
steps.text: Now use the idea on a new case. No people, no trees, just squares. Do not ask 'what object is hiding?' Ask 'what do the colors and order do to me?' That shift is how to look at abstract work.

guess.question: You see a painting that is only neat blue and yellow squares in a grid. What is the best plain description?
options: A secret horse you must find
A calm idea built from squares
guess.why: A calm idea built from squares is right, because there are no clues of a house or horse, only an ordered arrangement that can feel calm and steady.

steps.title: Why artists let go of things
steps.text: About a hundred years ago, artists like Wassily Kandinsky in Europe stopped trying to copy the outside world. They wanted painting to work more like music — no words or pictures needed, just sound and feeling. That choice gave us abstract painting.

steps.title: Look far, then close
steps.text: Next time, stand back, then step close. From far you feel the whole mood. Up close you see the hand — brush marks, layers, drips. Ask: what changed when I moved? That teaches you what the painting is really 'of.'

claims.text: A painting is colored material placed on a flat surface by a person.
Some paintings show things we can name, like a person or a house, and this is called representational art.
Abstract art uses colors, lines, and shapes that do not try to show a recognizable object or scene.
Abstract paintings can still mean something by creating feeling, movement, balance, or an idea through how the colors and shapes are arranged.
Artists including Wassily Kandinsky made some of the first fully abstract paintings in Europe in the 1910s.
